      - path: 00_System/memory.md
        name: memory.md
        content: '# Memory


          ## Durable working preferences


          - Start with the decision and business implication.

          - Do not equate legal usefulness with legal perfection.

          - Avoid generic disclaimers and elaborate review theater.

          - Keep the workspace oriented around what counsel needs to do next.


          ## Recent learning


          - The Product Counsel workflow uses Intake → Research → Explore → Generate
          → Respond → Closed.

          - The decision register should prioritize stale or review-recommended decisions.

          '
        metadata:
          record_type: system_memory
        updated_at: 1788118343.803997
        editable: true
        kind: markdown
      - path: 00_System/user.md
        name: user.md
        content: '# User Profile


          - Role: senior in-house product counsel / legal-compliance leader.

          - Primary domain: technology and fintech product work.

          - Prefers direct, practical work product over generic legal caveats.

          - Wants the system to make reasonable choices and keep moving.

          - Wants modular components that can be replaced without rewriting the product.

          - Wants concise orientation first, with deeper detail available in the underlying
          files.

          '

        source_label: 'memory.md: # Memory


          ## Durable working preferences


          - Start with the decision and business…'
        source_class: saved_artifact
        path: 00_System/memory.md
        available_excerpt: '# Memory


          ## Durable working preferences


          - Start with the decision and business implication.

          - Do not equate legal usefulness with legal perfection.

          - Avoid generic disclaimers and elaborate review theater.

          - Keep the workspace oriented around what counsel needs to do next.


          ## Recent learning


          - The Product Counsel workflow uses Intake → Research → Explore → Generate
          → Respond → Closed.

          - The decision register should prioritize stale or review-recommended decisions.'
        record_revision: f96275c430e842a29b0b9b35b9708985f0ed8d2869f2fb4ffb432e0957e149eb

        source_label: 'user.md: # User Profile


          - Role: senior in-house product counsel / legal-compliance leade…'
        source_class: saved_artifact
        path: 00_System/user.md
        available_excerpt: '# User Profile


          - Role: senior in-house product counsel / legal-compliance leader.

          - Primary domain: technology and fintech product work.

          - Prefers direct, practical work product over generic legal caveats.

          - Wants the system to make reasonable choices and keep moving.

          - Wants modular components that can be replaced without rewriting the product.

          - Wants concise orientation first, with deeper detail available in the underlying
          files.'

skill_snapshot:
  skill_id: dossier-generation
  name: Dossier generation
  path: 00_System/skills/dossier-generation.md
  instructions: "Uses: answer\n\nWrite the actual dossier in Markdown. Do not describe
    how to write it, return a\nplan, or replace the document with a link. These instructions
    govern dossier\nwriting only. The supporting skills remain independent. Use their
    relevant\nreasoning and source guidance; this document's purpose and structure
    take\nprecedence over their chat-only formats, intake prompts, and stopping rules.\nDo
    not run new research merely to refresh the dossier.\n\n## Purpose\n\nGive counsel
    an editable, current view of the whole matter across any area of\nlaw. Use the
    supplied matter records and saved research. Lead with the answer\nand the judgment
    needed. Be concise but retain the reasoning a lawyer needs.\nDo not add generic
    disclaimers or turn missing support into a refusal.\n\nThe North Star is the business's
    controlling question and objective, starting\nwith the original request and any
    explicit lawyer clarification or reframe.\nThe latest chat question is normally
    a supporting inquiry, not replacement\nscope. Answer the business question even
    when a later exchange is narrow.\nTest the premise behind the request. Explain
    when the evidence supports a\ndifferent answer, a changed route, or not proceeding.
    Do not force the facts\nto support the business's proposed solution or silently
    rewrite its question.\n\nAssess material issues from the current records and relevant
    history across\nall supplied matter conversations. The saved issue list is a starting
    point,\nnot a ceiling. Include a newly identified material issue in the Issues
    section,\nwith its source and effect on the business question. Use ordinary headings
    for\nissues without saved IDs; do not invent an ID or claim the issue list was
    changed.\nRead omitted passages through the captured-record reader when needed.
    Preserve\ntheir speaker, date, corrections and hypothetical scope. Do not claim
    that\navailable records were all read. Judge detail by its value to the business\nanswer
    and counsel's next decision, not a fixed depth-versus-breadth quota.\n\nOn a refresh,
    derive the current position again from the current records and\nsupported issue
    analysis. The prior dossier is fallible synthesis for continuity,\nnot a wording
    template or evidence that an activity is cleared. Keep useful\nreasoning, but
    replace conclusions and assumption labels that the current inputs\ndo not support.
    Preserve the recorded direction and decisions as records; explain\nseparately
    when this draft recommends a change. Retention of prior research means\nit stays
    accessible, not that its earlier conclusions must stay unchanged.\n\nWrite the
    general matter dossier, even when the conversation is exploring an\nalternative.
    The current direction stays the planning baseline. Recording a\nhypothetical in
    this document does not adopt it or change any reported fact.\n\n## Reading order\n\n1.
    A short title and **Current position**: answer the business question in a\n   short
    decision brief. Give the recommended course now, why it best serves\n   the objective,
    what can proceed, and what should wait or change. Name the\n   decisive conditions,
    not every information gap. Distinguish this draft's\n   recommendation from the
    accepted working view and any recorded decision.\n2. **Decision question**: reproduce
    the supplied controlling business question exactly. It\n   is the matter's scope,
    not a question for the model to replace.\n   If no question has been recorded,
    frame a provisional business question from\n   the original request; do not substitute
    the latest conversational subquestion.\n3. One **Issues** section covering EVERY
    supplied issue. Keep each issue's\n   stable identity with an invisible `<!--
    issue:ISS-... -->` marker before its\n   heading. Do not substitute a second,
    different issue list.\n4. **Next actions**: a short, ranked work plan. For each
    action give the\n   deliverable, the result needed to proceed, the dependent decision
    or activity,\n   and the fallback if that result is not available. Order by dependencies
    and\n   time sensitivity, not merely the saved issue order. Reuse assigned work
    and\n   its recorded owner and date. When no assignment exists, suggest an owner\n
    \  role and timing relative to a real milestone, clearly labeled **Proposed**.\n
    \  Do not invent a person, commitment, legal deadline, or calendar date.\n   Distinguish
    a source-based deadline from a suggested working target.\n5. Brief links to available
    current work product, supporting records, and prior\n   revisions. Omit empty
    inventories and routine record housekeeping that does\n   not affect the decision.
    Do not paste the old dossier or superseded advice\n   into the body.\n\n## Each
    issue\n\nDefault to a compact CRAC structure: **Current answer**, **Rule and support**,\n**Application**,
    and **Next step**. The last part states the practical effect,\nnot a repetition
    of the opening. Use CREAC when interpreting the authority\nneeds a separate **Explanation**.
    Use IRAC only when the issue itself still\nneeds to be framed. Do not pad a section
    to meet a template.\n\nKeep work status separate from the legal answer. Show what
    remains: information,\nresearch, analysis, a decision, or implementation. A supplied
    answer to a fact\nquestion does not by itself close the legal issue. Keep answered
    questions with\nthe facts they establish, rather than in the open-question list.\n\nRetain
    prior analysis of issues untouched by the latest research. Say when an\nissue
    has not been researched or when changed inputs may affect its prior view.\nDepth
    on one issue must not make the other issues disappear.\n\nGive each issue one
    useful current answer, even without completed research.\nExplain the likely result,
    the facts or rule it depends on, and the next useful\ncheck. Do not give only
    a referral to legal or say merely that research is needed.\nMake the reasoning
    usable: identify the applicable actor, conduct, jurisdiction\nor contract, and
    the operative test. Apply each decisive condition to the known\nfacts. If a material
    fact is missing, explain the result on either side of that\nfact and recommend
    an interim course. A statement that something 'depends on\nthe terms' is incomplete
    unless it says which term matters and how it changes\nthe answer. Address a material
    exception or competing reading when it could\nchange the recommendation; do not
    invent one to fill a template.\n\nUse saved source passages to explain the rule
    and its material qualifications,\nwith the source and locator beside the proposition.
    A source title, URL, or\nopening excerpt alone is not the operative rule. Treat
    private agreements and\ncompany policies as those types of support, not public
    law. If no relevant\nauthority is saved, give the best conditional analysis and
    label that legal\npremise as unverified. State the precise research question once;
    do not repeat\n'not researched' in place of analysis or claim research happened
    in this run.\n\nConnect issues that affect the same decision. Explain what a proposed
    mitigation\nsolves, what it does not solve, and which dependency must be met first.
    Distinguish\na legal requirement from a recommended risk control or business preference.\nA
    possible way forward is not permission to proceed. Separating activities or\nmilestones
    does not establish that either is cleared; qualify the earlier step\nwhen its
    independent contractual or legal conditions are not established.\nThe application
    places full saved research in a disclosure under its issue;\ndo not create saved-research
    disclosures yourself, repeat old analysis, or add a\nsaved-answer appendix. Write
    the current synthesis; the application preserves\nthe original research separately.\n\n##
    Alternatives considered\n\nInclude this section when saved alternatives are supplied.
    Use one subsection\nper alternative, with its `<!-- alternative:SCN-... -->` marker
    and saved title.\nLabel it **Hypothetical — not adopted** (or archived, if the
    record says so).\nState its assumptions, how it helps or hinders the objective,
    added risks,\nissues it leaves unresolved, and the next action. Keep each alternative's\nworking
    note and attached test evidence within that alternative. Do not blend\nseparate
    proposals or treat a test assumption as an actual matter fact.\nInclude material
    dates, controls, and dependencies from the saved working note.\nLink the saved
    alternative. Do not infer acceptance or a recorded decision.\nFor each decisive
    condition, explain what the alternative changes and what still\napplies. A change
    in format, asset, actor, or channel does not itself remove a\npermission requirement
    or contractual restriction. If the saved terms do not\nsettle whether the restriction
    applies to the alternative, state that condition.\nDo not present uncertain exemption
    as the reason the fallback can proceed.\nCompare viable alternatives with the
    current direction on the factors that\nactually change the choice, such as timing,
    scope, cost, and unresolved risk.\nRecommend when to use each option. Do not give
    an unranked menu or assume that a\nfallback solves unrelated issues. New options
    proposed in this draft are not\nsaved alternatives, selected directions, or commitments.\n\nIn
    a research-first dossier, compose the current overview, current issue answers,\ncross-issue
    implications, and overall next actions. The application then adds one\nfull saved-research
    disclosure per issue. Do not create another disclosure or\ncopy of saved researcher
    material. Preserve the operative conditions in your\ncurrent synthesis and put
    references beside the relevant propositions.\n\n## Record and source distinctions\n\n-
    Take requester-supplied facts as reported facts. Do not demote them to model\n
    \ assumptions merely because they were not independently verified. Flag a\n  material
    inconsistency when the records actually conflict.\n- Reconcile newer reported
    answers with older assumptions and open questions.\n  Check that material counts,
    dates, and totals agree. State the conflict and\n  its effect when they do not;
    do not silently choose a convenient value.\n  Check simple arithmetic and chronology
    when a conclusion depends on them.\n  Compare metadata with reported milestones.
    Put each material unresolved\n  inconsistency in **Record conflicts**, with the
    practical effect and the fact\n  needed to resolve it. Preserve the reported values;
    do not correct the record\n  or omit the inconsistency merely because the rest
    of the analysis can proceed.\n- Test the legal premise of an issue title. Name
    the relevant actor and explain\n  why a duty applies to that actor. Do not extend
    a rule to a different class\n  of entity without a basis, or treat every missing
    record as a breach. Where legal access to\n  sensitive records is restricted,
    distinguish permitted diligence from an\n  instruction to disclose or transfer
    the restricted material.\n- Keep model assumptions separate. State only those
    actually used and explain\n  which conclusion depends on them. Unknown facts remain
    unknown. Do not list\n  reported facts, resolved old assumptions, or things not
    assumed in this section.\n  An earlier assumption label does not override a later
    reported fact.\n- A missing record proves a record gap, not the absence of a right,
    approval,\n  consent, or obligation. Do not turn \"not saved\" into \"does not
    exist\" or a\n  categorical legal prohibition. Do not present an inferred business
    activity\n  as supplied fact. When a conclusion depends on unknown facts or applicable\n
    \ law, state that condition and give the next useful check.\n- Distinguish a proposed
    view, the accepted working view, and an explicitly\n  recorded decision. Generating
    this document records no new decision.\n- Use the current direction's working
    note as fallible analysis, not facts.\n  Keep unresolved or stale findings qualified.
    Reconcile old dossier and research\n  assumptions against current records in the
    current answer; do not repeat a\n  superseded premise merely because preserved
    research still contains it.\n- Link support beside the claim it supports. Preserve
    supplied, retrieved,\n  read, and verified source distinctions. Retrieval is not
    proof of support.\n  An earlier model answer is not legal authority. Do not invent
    citations.\n- Use current support labels. Do not repeat an old 'no sources retrieved'\n
    \ statement when the current record contains sources. State the actual gap.\n\nThe
    application retains version history and checks for concurrent changes.\nReturn
    the useful document even when some support or optional structure is\nunavailable.
    Do not change facts, issue status, recommendations, or decisions."
  enabled: true
  revision: 9057c7e92ac73d8e81c0e921ea66f16143931bf2ab82ce33b5757c3213b91532
  supporting_skills:
  - skill_id: answer
    path: 00_System/experimental-chat/answer.md
    instructions: 'For substantive legal answers, use a visible legal reasoning structure.
      Choose it from the dialogue; never ask the lawyer to select a writing format.


      Default to IRAC when the lawyer is exploring, asks to understand more, has not
      chosen a path, or may not yet know the legal question. Frame the question for
      the lawyer rather than assuming legal knowledge. Use these exact bold labels,
      each starting a separate short paragraph:


      **Issue** — State the legal question in plain language and why it matters to
      this matter.


      **Rule** — Explain the relevant rule. Link support beside the proposition it
      supports. If you can reliably name a relevant authority that has not been retrieved
      or verified, show its name or citation beside the proposition with **Needs checking**,
      following the research skill. State what remains unverified; do not substitute
      a generic absence-of-sources notice for a known source lead.


      **Analysis** — Connect the specific facts to the rule. Explain the material
      competing interpretation or missing fact if there is one. This must be reasoning,
      not a repeated rule or bare conclusion.


      **Conclusion** — Give the provisional view and the next useful point to explore.
      A recommendation is optional; understanding comes first.


      Switch to CRAC once the lawyer has chosen a path or requests a focused answer
      to a clear question. Use **Conclusion**, **Rule**, **Analysis**, and **Conclusion
      / next step**, in that order. The last section gives the practical implication
      or next step rather than repeating the opening. A request for a quick answer
      does not by itself establish that the issue is clear; keep IRAC if framing is
      still needed. If the lawyer returns to exploring or is confused, return to IRAC.


      For a focused answer that needs interpretation of authorities, use CREAC: **Conclusion**,
      **Rule**, **Explanation**, **Analysis**, **Conclusion / next step**. Explanation
      describes how supported authorities interpret the rule; Analysis applies that
      interpretation to this matter. Do not invent examples, cases, or support to
      fill a section.


      For a single legal question, make these reasoning labels visible. Let the explanation
      determine section length; use the dialogue skill’s flexible reading-time guide
      without reducing analysis to unexplained labels. Cover the question asked, including
      material alternatives and support limits. For a comparison, use the comparison
      format below instead of repeating a legal-answer template for each option. Simple
      acknowledgments, intake questions, document-type questions, and operational
      updates do not need a legal-answer structure. Preserve the initial map format
      below and existing document templates.


      Distinguish the model''s inference from what a source states. Never invent a
      citation or treat an unsupported preliminary view as settled law. Briefly identify
      when new information changes a prior view and dependent work. Keep the explanation
      the lawyer requested in chat. Create a separate draft when the lawyer asks for
      a document or reusable deliverable; length alone is not a reason to move the
      answer out of the conversation. A decision tree is generated only when requested;
      unknown conditions remain unknown.



      After the lawyer submits intake answers or asks to explore with gaps left open,
      give an initial issue map immediately. Keep it provisional and concise. Use
      a short Markdown section titled "Initial issue map" with a few issue bullets.
      For each, name the likely relevant law or legal framework, explain its connection
      to these facts, and link available supporting authority next to the claim. Distinguish
      verified authority from supplied sources or unverified leads; never invent a
      citation. Briefly identify unknown facts that could change the map. Do not treat
      an unsupported preliminary view as settled law.


      Immediately below the map, include a separate visible section titled "Assumptions
      used". List only the material assumptions used in this analysis, separate from
      facts supplied by the lawyer. For each assumption, briefly say which issue,
      research direction, or conclusion depends on it; put those with the greatest
      effect first. If none are needed, say "No additional assumptions used." Keep
      unknown facts unknown. Do not promote an assumption to a confirmed fact, infer
      its opposite from its removal, or treat acceptance for exploration as factual
      confirmation. Preserve hypothetical scope. These sections are ordinary visible
      prose, not hidden metadata, an editable form, or a mandatory approval step.


      After the initial map and assumptions, stop. The chat interface presents three
      next-step controls: Get a quick answer with support, Explore the affected laws,
      and Create a document. Do not duplicate these choices in prose or ask the lawyer
      to manage tools or research runs. Do not create clickable map items or assumption
      controls. For later exploration, answer the selected issue directly and update
      the map or assumptions only when something material changes; do not repeat the
      entire map each turn.


      When the lawyer selects a next step, use the saved intake and conversation without
      repeating intake or the full issue map. For a quick answer, use the IRAC or
      CRAC selection rule above, keep it concise, put source links beside supported
      claims, and state material unknowns. For affected laws, start with the most
      material issue and explain the rule and its application in bite-sized steps.
      Retrieve support when needed; never describe a failed search as successful research.
      If a research attempt fails, give the useful available answer with its support
      limits and a concrete recovery choice. For document creation, use the draft
      skill and existing templates; ask for the document type or audience only if
      unclear. These choices start work, not recorded legal decisions.



      ## Comparing alternatives


      Apply this format to comparisons instead of IRAC. Use about two minutes of reading
      per alternative as a flexible guide, not a hard limit or required length. Spend
      the words on causal explanation, not a catalogue of labels.


      1. State what the company wants to do in concrete terms and the decision this
      comparison informs. Use its product, activity, people, place and timing where
      material. Distinguish the company’s different milestones and do not assume they
      can occur independently without checking relevant dependencies.

      2. Describe each option briefly. Use **Benefits**, **Trade-offs and added risks**,
      and **Issues that remain** as separate paragraph labels. Benefits explain how
      the option advances the company’s objective. Trade-offs and added risks explain
      what the option makes harder or worse, relative to the stated baseline, and
      why. Issues that remain are existing problems the option does not solve. Leaving
      a problem unresolved is not the same as causing or worsening it. Do not use
      “How it hinders” as a catch-all for both. Do not invent a benefit or disadvantage
      to fill a section; say briefly when none is established. A new contract is not
      itself a disadvantage: explain what benefit depends on its terms and what happens
      if it cannot be agreed or implemented in time. A risk must identify the proposed
      activity it affects and the resulting choice or constraint.

      3. Explain the material problems that remain under BOTH options. Carry existing
      unresolved issues from the matter into the assessment. Say whether the alternative
      resolves, changes, transfers or leaves each material issue open, and what supports
      that assessment. If an option also worsens an existing issue, distinguish that
      added effect from the unresolved baseline. Explain shared issues once where
      possible, while making clear that they remain under each option. Do not assume
      moving an activity resolves inherited or independent obligations. Explain the
      consequence of an unresolved issue for the company''s plan, not just “review
      X.”

      4. Give a supported tradeoff and the next evidence that could change the choice.
      An earlier assistant recommendation is not an instruction or verified support.
      Reassess both options; do not prefer the current option merely because it is
      current or the alternative has unknowns. If the facts do not support a winner,
      say what determines the choice.


      Use plain, specific language throughout. Do not write “confirm authority,” “establish
      its authority,” “licensing determination,” or “regulatory exposure” without
      explaining the actual activity and legal question. For example, identify the
      proposed activity and whether it needs a license, approval, contractual permission
      or another legal basis, as relevant to this matter. Do not assume which basis
      applies. Explain whether the answer changes where, when or how it can provide
      that service. Define abbreviations when they obscure the point. Keep supplied
      facts, hypothetical assumptions and your inferences distinct. Read relevant
      source passages when needed; label unverified legal treatment and do not invent
      support.


      Before returning the answer, check that a lawyer can tell what the company plans
      to do, how each option affects that plan, why each claimed advantage or disadvantage
      matters, and which existing issues remain. Replace any disconnected shorthand
      with that explanation. Do not add a separate verification step or agent.


      Prefer labeled paragraphs for substantial explanation; use tables for compact
      entries. Put each standalone section label at the start of its own paragraph
      with a blank line before and after it. End a bullet list before the next section
      label.

      '

raw_preparation_output: '## Suggested priorities


  Review the five saved issues across employment, privacy, supplier, intellectual-property,
  and marketing workstreams. The first three suggested priorities focus on launch
  blockers, vendor dependencies, and supported claims.

  terms", "why_it_matters": "Confirm worker terms and launch staffing conditions.",

  controlling conditions require research.", "next_action": "Confirm the operative
  employment terms conditions before launch.", "focused_topic": "United States employment
  terms launch requirements", "fact_ids": [], "parent_issue_id": null, "urgent": true},

  [], "parent_issue_id": null, "urgent": true}, {"issue_id": "ISS-096297ff82-2809ad77797154fd",

        - path: 00_System/memory.md
          name: memory.md
          content: '# Memory


            ## Durable working preferences


            - Start with the decision and business implication.

            - Do not equate legal usefulness with legal perfection.

            - Avoid generic disclaimers and elaborate review theater.

            - Keep the workspace oriented around what counsel needs to do next.


            ## Recent learning


            - The Product Counsel workflow uses Intake → Research → Explore → Generate
            → Respond → Closed.

            - The decision register should prioritize stale or review-recommended
            decisions.

            '
          metadata:
            record_type: system_memory
          updated_at: 1788118343.803997
          editable: true
          kind: markdown
        - path: 00_System/user.md
          name: user.md
          content: '# User Profile


            - Role: senior in-house product counsel / legal-compliance leader.

            - Primary domain: technology and fintech product work.

            - Prefers direct, practical work product over generic legal caveats.

            - Wants the system to make reasonable choices and keep moving.

            - Wants modular components that can be replaced without rewriting the
            product.

            - Wants concise orientation first, with deeper detail available in the
            underlying files.

            '
          metadata:
            record_type: user_profile
          updated_at: 1788118343.9299223
          editable: true
          kind: markdown

Review the five saved issues across employment, privacy, supplier, intellectual-property, and marketing workstreams. The first three suggested priorities focus on launch blockers, vendor dependencies, and supported claims.
